    Regional Curve Standardization with dplPy¶

    Most detrending fits a separate growth curve to each series and divides it out. That works for closed-canopy, uniform-age stands, but it has a cost: a curve fit to one series cannot tell a slow climate trend from the tree's own growth trend, so it removes both. Any climate signal longer than the individual segments is lost. This is the segment-length curse.

    Regional Curve Standardization (RCS) breaks the curse. Instead of one curve per series, it aligns every series by cambial age (rings counted from the pith), averages them into a single regional curve that describes the average biological growth trend for the site, and divides each series by the slice of that one curve matching its own ages. Because the regional curve is common to all trees, climate trends longer than any single series survive. RCS is the method of choice for long, composite, and subfossil collections, where recovering multi-centennial climate is the whole point.

    dplPy offers four members of the RCS family:

    • rcs — the classic single regional curve.
    • sfrcs — signal-free RCS, which removes the common climate signal's imprint on the regional curve before standardizing.
    • mrcs — multiple-curve RCS, one regional curve per growth-rate class.
    • sfmrcs — signal-free multiple-curve RCS, the two ideas combined.

    This notebook works through all four on a real subfossil collection: the Taimyr (TAI) Siberian larch set from Büntgen et al. (2021), read straight from the ITRDB. It is 356 series spanning 207 BC to AD 2011 — exactly the kind of long, composite material RCS is built for. Along the way we poke the functions a little, since they are new.

    Copied! 
    import dplpy as dpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

%matplotlib inline

    1. Read the collection from the ITRDB¶

    readers takes a URL, so we pull the Taimyr file directly from the NOAA archive. Swap the site code in the URL for another Büntgen 2021 site (for example NYA_all.rwl, the largest) to run the same notebook on different data.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    URL = "https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/paleo/treering/reconstructions/buentgen2021/TAI_all.rwl"
rwl = dpl.readers(URL)
    URL = "https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/paleo/treering/reconstructions/buentgen2021/TAI_all.rwl" rwl = dpl.readers(URL)
    TAI_all.rwl successfully extracted as rwl file with 356 series covering the period from -207 to 2011

    2. Check for oddities¶

    Before standardizing anything, screen the collection with dpl.check. For a subfossil larch set we expect a lot of zero rings (locally absent rings, a real and common feature of these trees), so those show up as notes, not errors.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    findings = dpl.check(rwl)
findings.groupby(["group", "severity"]).size()
    findings = dpl.check(rwl) findings.groupby(["group", "severity"]).size()
    Out[4]:
    group        severity
crossdating  note         1
             warning     14
zeros        note        83
dtype: int64

    The zero-ring notes are the locally absent rings, which are genuine data and are kept. The crossdating group flags a handful of series that fit the collection less well than the rest — worth a look in a real study, but not a barrier to the demonstration here. Indeed, most of these aren't too concerning, except series 03 236, which deserves closer scrutiny.

    3. Verify the collection crossdates¶

    These are published, already-crossdated data, so this is a sanity check rather than a re-dating. The mean interseries correlation is the single number that summarizes how strongly the series share a common signal; a healthy site sits around 0.5 or higher.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    mean_corr = dpl.interseries_corr(rwl)["mean"]
mean_corr # collection-wide mean interseries correlation
    mean_corr = dpl.interseries_corr(rwl)["mean"] mean_corr # collection-wide mean interseries correlation
    Out[6]:
    0.671

    4. A note on pith offsets¶

    RCS aligns series by cambial age, so in principle it needs each series' pith offset — how many rings are missing between the innermost measured ring and the true pith. This file ships no offset table, so we use dplPy's default: every series is treated as pith-present (po=0), aligning by the first measured ring. That is the standard fallback when offsets are not archived, and it is what most published RCS chronologies without pith estimates assume.

    If you do have offsets, pass them as po= (a {series: offset} map or a two-column table). dplPy's pith_offset is a true offset: 0 means the pith is present. (dplR's po is the cambial age of the first ring, where 1 means pith present, so subtract 1 from a dplR table.)

    5. rcs: the single regional curve¶

    rcs fits one regional curve to the age-aligned collection and divides each series by it. The defaults are dplPy's modern choices: an age-dependent spline for the curve (fit="AgeDepSpline"), the ratio method (method="ratio"), and a non-increasing old-age end (pos_slope=False, faithful to ARSTAN and CRUST). plot=True draws dplPy's RCS figure: the regional curve and the resulting chronology.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    rwi_rcs = dpl.rcs(rwl, plot=True)
plt.show()
    rwi_rcs = dpl.rcs(rwl, plot=True) plt.show()

    The regional curve itself is the heart of the method. We can include it in the output by adding rc_out=True to the input parameters and then plot it against cambial age — the classic negative-exponential-like decline of ring width as a tree grows older.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    out = dpl.rcs(rwl, rc_out=True, plot=False)
rc = out["rc"] # from the output, extract just the regional curve

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.5))
plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(rc) + 1), rc, color="b") # plot just the regional curve
plt.xlabel("Cambial age (rings from pith)"); plt.ylabel("Ring width (mm)")
plt.title("TAI regional curve")
plt.show()
    out = dpl.rcs(rwl, rc_out=True, plot=False) rc = out["rc"] # from the output, extract just the regional curve plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.5)) plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(rc) + 1), rc, color="b") # plot just the regional curve plt.xlabel("Cambial age (rings from pith)"); plt.ylabel("Ring width (mm)") plt.title("TAI regional curve") plt.show()

    Poking rcs: ratio vs difference, and the old-age slope¶

    Two switches are worth seeing. method="difference" subtracts the curve instead of dividing by it (the variance-stabilized choice); pos_slope=True lets the regional curve rise again at great age instead of being held non-increasing. We compare the regional curves under the default and pos_slope=True.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    rc_default = dpl.rcs(rwl, rc_out=True, plot=False)["rc"] # appending the ["rc"] at the end returns only the regional curve
rc_posslope = dpl.rcs(rwl, pos_slope=True, rc_out=True, plot=False)["rc"] # appending the ["rc"] at the end returns only the regional curve

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.5))
plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(rc_default) + 1), rc_default, color="b", label="pos_slope=False (default)")
plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(rc_posslope) + 1), rc_posslope, color="r", lw=1, label="pos_slope=True")
plt.xlabel("Cambial age"); plt.ylabel("Ring width (mm)"); plt.title("Old-age end of the regional curve")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
    rc_default = dpl.rcs(rwl, rc_out=True, plot=False)["rc"] # appending the ["rc"] at the end returns only the regional curve rc_posslope = dpl.rcs(rwl, pos_slope=True, rc_out=True, plot=False)["rc"] # appending the ["rc"] at the end returns only the regional curve plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.5)) plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(rc_default) + 1), rc_default, color="b", label="pos_slope=False (default)") plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(rc_posslope) + 1), rc_posslope, color="r", lw=1, label="pos_slope=True") plt.xlabel("Cambial age"); plt.ylabel("Ring width (mm)"); plt.title("Old-age end of the regional curve") plt.legend() plt.show()
    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    # ratio and difference give different indices; both are valid, for different aims
rwi_ratio = dpl.rcs(rwl, method="ratio", plot=False) # divide series by regional curve
rwi_diff = dpl.rcs(rwl, method="difference", plot=False) # subtract regional curve from series
rwi_ratio.mean(axis=1).mean(), rwi_diff.mean(axis=1).mean()   # ratios (division) center near 1, differences (subtraction) near 0
    # ratio and difference give different indices; both are valid, for different aims rwi_ratio = dpl.rcs(rwl, method="ratio", plot=False) # divide series by regional curve rwi_diff = dpl.rcs(rwl, method="difference", plot=False) # subtract regional curve from series rwi_ratio.mean(axis=1).mean(), rwi_diff.mean(axis=1).mean() # ratios (division) center near 1, differences (subtraction) near 0
    Out[10]:
    (np.float64(1.0884405564083905), np.float64(0.021503073348939437))

    6. sfrcs: signal-free RCS¶

    There is a subtlety in RCS. The regional curve is an average over all series, so a strong common climate signal leaves its fingerprint in the curve itself, which then gets divided back out of the indices — biasing the result, especially the low-frequency trend and the recent end where sample depth changes. Signal-free standardization (Melvin & Briffa) breaks the circularity: it estimates the curve, removes the common signal, re-estimates the curve from the signal-free series, and iterates until the curve stops changing.

    sfrcs runs that iteration around the RCS curve.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    rwi_sfrcs = dpl.sfrcs(rwl, plot=True)
plt.show()
    rwi_sfrcs = dpl.sfrcs(rwl, plot=True) plt.show()
    Signal-free RCS converged in 4 iterations (max change 5.95e-04 < 0.001).

    The signal-free curve, side by side¶

    Plotting the two regional curves together shows what the signal-free pass changed. On TAI the curves are close, so the common signal left only a modest imprint, but they separate at the young, fast-growth end, where the signal-free estimate sits a little higher. That difference is small in millimetres yet it is exactly the kind of low-frequency adjustment that carries through into the chronology.

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    rc_rcs = dpl.rcs(rwl, rc_out=True, plot=False)["rc"]
rc_sfrcs = dpl.sfrcs(rwl, return_info=True, plot=False)["rc"]   # signal-free curve

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.5))
plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(rc_rcs) + 1), rc_rcs, color="b", label="rcs")
plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(rc_sfrcs) + 1), rc_sfrcs, color="r", lw=1, label="sfrcs")
plt.xlabel("Cambial age"); plt.ylabel("Ring width (mm)"); plt.title("Regional curve: rcs vs sfrcs")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
    rc_rcs = dpl.rcs(rwl, rc_out=True, plot=False)["rc"] rc_sfrcs = dpl.sfrcs(rwl, return_info=True, plot=False)["rc"] # signal-free curve plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.5)) plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(rc_rcs) + 1), rc_rcs, color="b", label="rcs") plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(rc_sfrcs) + 1), rc_sfrcs, color="r", lw=1, label="sfrcs") plt.xlabel("Cambial age"); plt.ylabel("Ring width (mm)"); plt.title("Regional curve: rcs vs sfrcs") plt.legend() plt.show()
    Signal-free RCS converged in 4 iterations (max change 5.95e-04 < 0.001).

    7. mrcs: multiple regional curves¶

    A single regional curve assumes every tree follows the same average growth trend. But fast- and slow-growing trees have differently shaped curves, and if the mix of fast- and slow-growers changes over time — as it does when a subfossil collection shifts from one period to another — a single average curve injects a spurious trend. This is modern (or differing-contemporaneous) sample bias.

    mrcs (the CRUST approach of Melvin & Briffa) sorts the trees by growth rate, splits them into n_curves equal classes, and builds one regional curve per class. Each tree is standardized by the curve for its own class.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    rwi_mrcs = dpl.mrcs(rwl, n_curves=3, plot=True)
plt.show()
    rwi_mrcs = dpl.mrcs(rwl, n_curves=3, plot=True) plt.show()

    The point of mrcs is clearest when we overlay the class curves on the single curve. The fast-growth class sits well above the slow-growth class; the single curve is a blend whose shape depends on how many of each are in the sample at a given time.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    mout = dpl.mrcs(rwl, n_curves=3, rc_out=True, plot=False)
curves = mout["rc"]                    # one regional curve per growth class

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.5))
plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(rc) + 1), rc, color="black", lw=2, label="single curve (rcs)")
for k, c in enumerate(curves):
    plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(c) + 1), c, lw=1, label=f"class {k + 1}")
plt.xlabel("Cambial age"); plt.ylabel("Ring width (mm)"); plt.title("One curve vs three growth-class curves")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
    mout = dpl.mrcs(rwl, n_curves=3, rc_out=True, plot=False) curves = mout["rc"] # one regional curve per growth class plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.5)) plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(rc) + 1), rc, color="black", lw=2, label="single curve (rcs)") for k, c in enumerate(curves): plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(c) + 1), c, lw=1, label=f"class {k + 1}") plt.xlabel("Cambial age"); plt.ylabel("Ring width (mm)"); plt.title("One curve vs three growth-class curves") plt.legend() plt.show()
    In [15]:
    Copied! 
    # how many trees landed in each growth class?
pd.Series(mout["alloc"]).value_counts().sort_index()
    # how many trees landed in each growth class? pd.Series(mout["alloc"]).value_counts().sort_index()
    Out[15]:

1    119
2    118

    8. sfmrcs: signal-free multiple-curve RCS¶

    The two refinements are independent, so they combine: sfmrcs runs the signal-free iteration around the multiple-curve allocation. It is the most elaborate member of the family.

    In [16]:
    Copied! 
    rwi_sfmrcs = dpl.sfmrcs(rwl, n_curves=3, plot=True)
plt.show()
    rwi_sfmrcs = dpl.sfmrcs(rwl, n_curves=3, plot=True) plt.show()
    Signal-free RCS converged in 4 iterations (max change 5.03e-04 < 0.001).

    9. The family nests¶

    mrcs and sfmrcs are strict generalizations: with a single class they must reduce exactly to rcs and sfrcs. This is both a design property worth knowing and a correctness check worth running.

    In [17]:
    Copied! 
    a = dpl.mrcs(rwl, n_curves=1, plot=False)
b = dpl.rcs(rwl, plot=False)
print("mrcs(n_curves=1) == rcs    max abs diff:", float(np.nanmax(np.abs(a.values - b.values))))

c = dpl.sfmrcs(rwl, n_curves=1, plot=False)
d = dpl.sfrcs(rwl, plot=False)
print("sfmrcs(n_curves=1) == sfrcs max abs diff:", float(np.nanmax(np.abs(c.values - d.values))))
    a = dpl.mrcs(rwl, n_curves=1, plot=False) b = dpl.rcs(rwl, plot=False) print("mrcs(n_curves=1) == rcs max abs diff:", float(np.nanmax(np.abs(a.values - b.values)))) c = dpl.sfmrcs(rwl, n_curves=1, plot=False) d = dpl.sfrcs(rwl, plot=False) print("sfmrcs(n_curves=1) == sfrcs max abs diff:", float(np.nanmax(np.abs(c.values - d.values))))
    mrcs(n_curves=1) == rcs    max abs diff: 0.0
Signal-free RCS converged in 4 iterations (max change 5.95e-04 < 0.001).

    Signal-free RCS converged in 4 iterations (max change 5.95e-04 < 0.001).
sfmrcs(n_curves=1) == sfrcs max abs diff: 0.0

    10. Comparing the four chronologies¶

    The real test is what the chronologies look like. We build a standard chronology from each set of indices with chron, then overlay them. To see the low-frequency behaviour — the part RCS exists to preserve — we smooth each with a 20-year running mean and show the well-replicated portion (sample depth at least five series).

    In [18]:
    Copied! 
    variants = {
    "rcs": rwi_rcs,
    "sfrcs": rwi_sfrcs,
    "mrcs (3)": rwi_mrcs,
    "sfmrcs (3)": rwi_sfmrcs,
}

crns = {name: dpl.chron(rwi, plot=False) for name, rwi in variants.items()}
    variants = { "rcs": rwi_rcs, "sfrcs": rwi_sfrcs, "mrcs (3)": rwi_mrcs, "sfmrcs (3)": rwi_sfmrcs, } crns = {name: dpl.chron(rwi, plot=False) for name, rwi in variants.items()}
    In [19]:
    Copied! 
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
for name, crn in crns.items():
    well = crn[crn["samp_depth"] >= 5]           # drop thinly-replicated ends
    plt.plot(well.index, well["std"].rolling(20, center=True).mean(), lw=1, label=name)
plt.axhline(1.0, color="grey", lw=0.6)
plt.xlabel("Year"); plt.ylabel("Index (20-yr running mean)")
plt.title("TAI chronology under four RCS variants")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4)) for name, crn in crns.items(): well = crn[crn["samp_depth"] >= 5] # drop thinly-replicated ends plt.plot(well.index, well["std"].rolling(20, center=True).mean(), lw=1, label=name) plt.axhline(1.0, color="grey", lw=0.6) plt.xlabel("Year"); plt.ylabel("Index (20-yr running mean)") plt.title("TAI chronology under four RCS variants") plt.legend() plt.show()

    The four chronologies agree on the high-frequency, year-to-year signal and diverge mostly (although still minimally) in the low-frequency trend — which is exactly where the method choice matters. Signal-free standardization and multiple curves each adjust the long-term shape, and the differences you see are the sample-bias corrections those methods are designed to make.

    Choosing among them¶

    • rcs — the baseline. One regional curve, the method's original form.
    • sfrcs — when you want to remove the common signal's bias from the curve, especially for the low-frequency trend and the recent end.
    • mrcs — when the growth-rate mix of the sample changes through time, which risks a spurious trend from a single blended curve.
    • sfmrcs — both corrections at once.

    All four share the same fit, method, period, and pos_slope vocabulary as detrend and rcs, so anything you learned tuning one carries over. Pith offsets, when you have them, go in po= and matter most for the shape of the young end of every curve.

    See the detrending and standardization guide for the curve-fitting options, and the fidelity notes for how dplPy's RCS follows ARSTAN and CRUST.
